evidence.text: Atelectasis can happen for several reasons, including airway blockage, compression from nearby fluid or air, shallow breathing, or postoperative changes. Small areas may cause few symptoms, while larger areas can be associated with shortness of breath, faster breathing, low oxygen, or reduced movement on the affected side. On chest X-ray, atelectasis is often considered when there is increased opacity together with signs of volume loss. Depending on the location, this may include crowding of nearby structures, elevation of the diaphragm, shift of fissures, or movement of the mediastinum toward the affected side.

evidence.text: On chest X-ray, pleural effusion is usually considered when there is abnormal fluid at the lung base or in the pleural space. It may appear with blunting of the costophrenic angle, dependent layering fluid, or a horizontal air-fluid level if both air and fluid are present. Lateral decubitus views can show smaller amounts of fluid than an upright chest X-ray. Pleural effusion matters because it can reduce lung expansion and may be associated with shortness of breath, chest pain, or cough.

evidence.text: Consolidation is a radiographic pattern where normally air-filled lung tissue becomes filled with material such as inflammatory fluid, pus, blood, edema, or other liquid.
